question: Which four categories of licensees does ORC 4735.091 name as eligible to be associated with a brokerage as either an employee or an independent contractor?
choice_a: Real estate brokers, real estate salespersons, foreign real estate dealers, and foreign real estate salespersons
choice_b: Only real estate salespersons and property managers
choice_c: Only real estate brokers and licensed appraisers
choice_d: Real estate brokers, salespersons, and title agents, but not foreign real estate licensees
explanation: ORC 4735.091's text names four categories -- real estate broker, real estate salesperson, foreign real estate dealer, and foreign real estate salesperson -- as licensees who may be associated with a brokerage as either an employee or an independent contractor.

question: Under ORC 4735.091, what must every covered licensee be associated with, regardless of whether they choose the employee or independent-contractor structure?
choice_a: A brokerage -- the statute allows the licensee to be associated "with a brokerage" as either an employee or an independent contractor, not to work unaffiliated with any brokerage
choice_b: The Ohio Division of Real Estate directly, bypassing any brokerage
choice_c: A multiple listing service, which substitutes for brokerage affiliation
choice_d: No entity at all -- independent contractors under 4735.091 need no brokerage affiliation
explanation: ORC 4735.091's text is that the licensee "may be associated with a brokerage as either an employee or an independent contractor" -- brokerage affiliation itself is the constant; only the structure of that affiliation is a choice.

question: Does ORC 4735.091 itself supply or control the federal tax-law test (such as the IRS common-law factors) for whether a licensee qualifies as an independent contractor?
choice_a: No -- ORC 4735.091 only authorizes either arrangement as a matter of Ohio real estate license law; it does not supply or override the separate federal tax-classification test
choice_b: Yes -- it adopts the IRS's independent-contractor factors verbatim into Ohio license law
choice_c: Yes -- it requires the Ohio Division of Real Estate to issue a binding federal tax ruling for each licensee
choice_d: No, because ORC 4735.091 has been superseded entirely by federal tax law
explanation: ORC 4735.091 addresses only whether Ohio license law permits an employee or independent-contractor structure between broker and licensee; it does not purport to establish or displace the separate federal tax-classification analysis that governs withholding and reporting obligations.

question: A newly licensed broker decides to structure every salesperson at the brokerage strictly as a W-2 employee, offering no independent-contractor option. Is this compliant with ORC 4735.091?
choice_a: Yes -- ORC 4735.091 makes the employee-or-independent-contractor choice permissive, so a broker who uses only the employee model for all salespersons is not violating the statute
choice_b: No -- the broker must offer both structures, and omitting the independent-contractor option is itself a violation
choice_c: No -- only foreign real estate dealers and foreign real estate salespersons may be classified as employees
choice_d: No -- ORC 4735.091 requires every real estate salesperson to be classified as an independent contractor by default
explanation: Because the statute uses permissive language authorizing either structure, a brokerage may lawfully choose to use the employee model exclusively (or the independent-contractor model exclusively) -- ORC 4735.091 does not obligate a broker to offer both options to every licensee.

question: Which licensee category is explicitly named in ORC 4735.091 alongside real estate brokers and real estate salespersons?
choice_a: Foreign real estate dealers and foreign real estate salespersons
choice_b: Property managers and leasing agents
choice_c: Home inspectors and licensed appraisers
choice_d: Escrow officers and title agents
explanation: ORC 4735.091 names four specific categories -- broker, salesperson, foreign real estate dealer, and foreign real estate salesperson -- as licensees who may choose either employee or independent-contractor association with a brokerage; property managers, inspectors, appraisers, escrow officers, and title agents are not covered by this provision.

question: What word in ORC 4735.091's text signals that the employee/independent-contractor choice is optional rather than a mandated single structure?
choice_a: "May" -- the statute states a licensee "may be associated ... as either an employee or an independent contractor," permissive language rather than a mandate
choice_b: "Shall," which mandates the independent-contractor structure exclusively
choice_c: "Must," which mandates the employee structure exclusively
choice_d: The statute contains no permissive language -- one arrangement is compulsory for all licensees
explanation: ORC 4735.091 is phrased permissively ("may be associated ... as either"), which is why Ohio license law does not compel one structure over the other and instead leaves the choice to the broker and licensee.

question: Precisely which two duties does ORC 4735.18(A)(31) require a broker to perform, within a reasonable time after receiving a commission?
choice_a: Both render an accounting to, and pay, the real estate salesperson the salesperson's earned share
choice_b: Only pay the salesperson -- no accounting of the commission is legally required
choice_c: Only render an accounting -- the timing of actual payment is unregulated
choice_d: File a report with the Ohio Division of Real Estate within 30 days of the closing
explanation: ORC 4735.18(A)(31)'s text covers failure "to render an accounting to and pay a real estate salesperson" -- it imposes two distinct duties, accounting and payment, not payment alone.

question: Under ORC 4735.18(A)(31), what event starts the "reasonable time" clock for the broker's duty to account for and pay a salesperson's earned commission share?
choice_a: The broker's receipt of the commission -- the duty runs from when the broker actually receives the commission, not from the closing date or contract-signing date
choice_b: The date the listing agreement was originally signed
choice_c: The date the purchase contract was executed, regardless of when the commission funds are actually received
choice_d: The salesperson's written demand for payment, which the statute requires before any duty arises
explanation: The statute's text ties the duty to a reasonable time "after the receipt of the commission by the broker" -- the broker's actual receipt of funds is the triggering event, not an earlier contractual milestone or a demand by the salesperson.

question: A broker receives a commission at closing and eventually pays the affiliated salesperson the correct earned share, but never sends the salesperson any statement showing how that share was calculated. Has the broker violated ORC 4735.18(A)(31)?
choice_a: Yes -- the statute requires both rendering an accounting and paying; omitting the accounting is independently disciplinable even if the payment itself is accurate and timely
choice_b: No -- only a late or missing payment violates the statute, not missing paperwork
choice_c: No -- an accounting is required only if the salesperson makes a written request for one
choice_d: No -- ORC 4735.18(A)(31) applies only when there is a dispute over the dollar amount owed
explanation: Because ORC 4735.18(A)(31) imposes two separate duties -- render an accounting and pay -- a broker who pays correctly but never accounts for how the share was calculated has still failed one of the two statutory duties.

question: Under ORC 4735.18(A)(31), a broker's duty to pay a salesperson's earned commission share does not arise until which event has occurred?
choice_a: The broker has actually received the commission from the transaction
choice_b: The buyer has taken physical possession of the property
choice_c: The title company has issued a final title insurance policy
choice_d: Thirty days have elapsed since the purchase contract was executed
explanation: The statute's reasonable-time duty is expressly conditioned on "receipt of the commission by the broker" -- there is no independent duty to pay before the broker has the funds in hand, regardless of possession, title-policy issuance, or elapsed calendar time.

question: Who is empowered to investigate and who is empowered to impose discipline for a broker's violation of ORC 4735.18(A)(31)?
choice_a: The superintendent of real estate may investigate the licensee's conduct, and the Ohio real estate commission may impose the disciplinary sanction
choice_b: A county court of common pleas both investigates and imposes discipline
choice_c: The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development investigates and disciplines Ohio licensees under this section
choice_d: Only a civil jury, following a private lawsuit by the salesperson, may impose any sanction
explanation: ORC 4735.18(A)'s opening framework authorizes the superintendent of real estate to investigate licensee conduct, with the Ohio real estate commission imposing disciplinary sanctions for the enumerated grounds, including the (A)(31) commission-accounting-and-payment duty.

question: ORC 4735.18(A)(31)'s duty to account for and pay an earned commission share runs specifically in favor of which party?
choice_a: A real estate salesperson who is owed an earned share of a commission the broker has received
choice_b: The buyer in the underlying real estate transaction
choice_c: The seller's mortgage lender
choice_d: Any unlicensed referral source who informally assisted with the sale
explanation: The statute's text names "a real estate salesperson" as the party owed the accounting and payment -- it protects the affiliated salesperson's earned commission share, not buyers, lenders, or unlicensed referral sources.

question: How does the accounting duty in ORC 4735.18(A)(31) differ from the accounting duty in the neighboring ORC 4735.18(A)(30)?
choice_a: (A)(31) requires accounting for and payment of a salesperson's earned commission share, while (A)(30) requires a prompt, complete statement of expenditures of funds a broker or salesperson advanced on behalf of a party to a transaction -- two distinct disciplinable accounting duties
choice_b: The two subsections are identical and both apply exclusively to escrow-account disputes
choice_c: (A)(30) applies only to commission payments, while (A)(31) applies only to expense reimbursements
choice_d: (A)(30) has been repealed and its content fully consolidated into (A)(31)
explanation: ORC 4735.18(A)(30) addresses a broker's or salesperson's duty to promptly account for funds advanced by or on behalf of a transaction party, while (A)(31) separately addresses accounting for and paying a salesperson's own earned commission share -- distinct duties enumerated as separate disciplinable grounds.

question: Under ORC 4735.18(A)(39), must a right-to-list home sale agreement actually be enforced against the homeowner on a later sale for the broker to be subject to discipline?
choice_a: No -- the statute's language is triggered by "entering into" such an agreement; enforcement or invocation of the clause is not a stated element of the violation
choice_b: Yes -- discipline attaches only once the broker actually invokes the right-to-list clause on a future, unrelated sale
choice_c: Yes -- discipline attaches only once the homeowner files a written complaint about the clause
choice_d: No -- but only if the agreement is also recorded with the county recorder of deeds
explanation: ORC 4735.18(A)(39) reads as prohibiting "entering into" a right-to-list home sale agreement -- the act of entering into it is what the statute targets, not whether the clause is later enforced or recorded.

question: ORC 4735.18(A)(39)'s right-to-list prohibition is one of approximately how many enumerated disciplinable grounds listed under ORC 4735.18(A)?
choice_a: Approximately 40 enumerated grounds
choice_b: Exactly 5 enumerated grounds
choice_c: Approximately 200 enumerated grounds
choice_d: ORC 4735.18(A) lists no specific grounds, only a general standard of "unprofessional conduct"
explanation: ORC 4735.18(A) enumerates roughly 40 specific disciplinable grounds, of which the right-to-list prohibition at (A)(39) is one named, freestanding provision among many others addressing recordkeeping, escrow, advertising, commission payment, and similar conduct.

question: A homeowner and broker execute an ordinary exclusive-right-to-sell listing agreement, with a definite expiration date, that governs only the current sale and creates no obligation regarding any future, unrelated sale. Does this agreement fall within ORC 4735.18(A)(39)'s prohibition?
choice_a: No -- ORC 4735.18(A)(39) targets "right-to-list" home-sale agreements specifically, a distinct named practice, not an ordinary exclusive listing agreement limited to the current transaction
choice_b: Yes -- any exclusive-right-to-sell agreement is automatically treated as a prohibited right-to-list agreement
choice_c: Yes -- because the agreement does not name a fixed commission percentage
choice_d: Yes -- because exclusive listing agreements always bind the homeowner to future, unrelated sales
explanation: A standard exclusive listing agreement confined to the current transaction, with a proper expiration date, is not the type of restrictive future-sale-binding arrangement ORC 4735.18(A)(39) prohibits -- the prohibition is aimed at the distinct "right-to-list" practice, not ordinary exclusive listings.

question: Within ORC 4735.18(A)'s roughly 40 enumerated grounds, is the right-to-list prohibition at (A)(39) grouped as part of the escrow/trust-account provisions, or does it stand as an independent, specifically named prohibition?
choice_a: It is a standalone prohibition targeting one particular type of restrictive agreement, distinct from the escrow and trust-account provisions found elsewhere in ORC 4735.18(A) and ORC 4735.24
choice_b: It is part of the same escrow-accounting ground as (A)(30) and cannot be charged independently
choice_c: It automatically repeals ORC 4735.24's earnest-money escrow requirements
choice_d: It applies only when combined with a separate escrow-account violation
explanation: ORC 4735.18(A)(39) is its own freestanding, specifically named ground among the chapter's roughly 40 enumerated grounds -- it does not depend on, and is not grouped with, the escrow or trust-account provisions found in other subsections or in ORC 4735.24.

question: Besides stating compensation is negotiable, what statement must ORC 4735.55 require a written agency agreement to include regarding a named discriminatory practice?
choice_a: A statement defining "blockbusting" and stating that the practice is illegal
choice_b: A statement defining "redlining" and requiring separate lender disclosure
choice_c: A statement waiving the client's right to sue for housing discrimination
choice_d: A statement that blockbusting is permitted only with the client's written consent
explanation: ORC 4735.55 requires the written agency agreement to include a statement defining blockbusting and declaring it illegal, as one of several required disclosure elements alongside negotiable-compensation language and the HUD equal housing logotype.

question: ORC 4735.55 requires a written agency agreement to include a copy of which federal logotype, and what federal regulation specifies that logotype?
choice_a: The United States Department of Housing and Urban Development's equal housing opportunity logotype, as set forth in 24 C.F.R. 109.30
choice_b: The Federal Trade Commission's consumer-protection seal, as set forth in 16 C.F.R. 233
choice_c: The Department of Justice's fair-lending seal, as set forth in 28 C.F.R. 42
choice_d: A private trade association's Realtor trademark logo
explanation: ORC 4735.55 requires a copy of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's equal housing opportunity logotype, as set forth in 24 C.F.R. 109.30, to be included in the written agency agreement -- a specific, federally-defined graphic requirement.

question: ORC 4735.55 requires the written agency agreement to include a fair housing compliance statement referencing which federal statute?
choice_a: The federal Fair Housing Act, codified at 42 U.S.C.A. 3601, along with applicable Ohio fair-housing law
choice_b: The federal Truth in Lending Act, 15 U.S.C. 1601
choice_c: The federal Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act, 12 U.S.C. 2601
choice_d: The federal Equal Credit Opportunity Act, 15 U.S.C. 1691
explanation: ORC 4735.55 requires the agreement to reference fair housing law compliance, citing the federal Fair Housing Act at 42 U.S.C.A. 3601 together with applicable Ohio fair-housing law, distinct from lending-disclosure statutes like TILA, RESPA, or ECOA.

question: In addition to compensation and fair-housing disclosures, what must ORC 4735.55 require a written agency agreement to state about the agency relationship being created?
choice_a: That the licensee is appointed as an agent, and whether that appointment is exclusive or nonexclusive
choice_b: Whether the agent holds a real estate license reciprocal with another state
choice_c: Whether the agent carries errors-and-omissions insurance coverage
choice_d: The agent's total number of closed transactions during the prior calendar year
explanation: ORC 4735.55 requires the written agreement to state that the licensee is appointed as agent and whether that appointment is exclusive or nonexclusive -- distinct from the compensation, blockbusting, and fair-housing disclosure elements addressed elsewhere in the same section.

question: What execution formalities does ORC 4735.55 impose on a written agency agreement, beyond its required disclosure content?
choice_a: It must be signed and dated by both parties, with copies provided to the client
choice_b: It must be notarized by a licensed Ohio notary public
choice_c: It must be recorded with the county recorder within 30 days of signing
choice_d: It must be co-signed by the principal broker of every brokerage involved in the transaction
explanation: ORC 4735.55 requires the written agreement to be signed and dated by both parties, with copies furnished to the client -- there is no notarization or county-recording requirement imposed by this section.

question: A buyer representation agreement conspicuously discloses that the buyer's agent's commission "may be paid by the seller, a third party, or through a co-brokerage split with the listing broker," but the agreement is silent on blockbusting and includes no HUD equal housing logotype. What is the compliance problem under ORC 4735.55?
choice_a: The agreement satisfies the compensation-negotiability language but omits two other required elements -- the blockbusting statement and the HUD equal housing opportunity logotype
choice_b: There is no compliance problem, since only compensation language is a required element
choice_c: The agreement is invalid solely because a third party may be permitted to pay the commission
choice_d: The HUD logotype is optional under ORC 4735.55 for any agreement covering a buyer rather than a seller
explanation: ORC 4735.55 lists several independently required elements -- negotiable-compensation language, a blockbusting statement, and the HUD equal housing logotype among them -- so satisfying one element does not excuse omitting the others.

question: Under ORC 4735.55, may a written agency agreement disclose that a cooperating broker will "split" or "share" the commission as part of the agreed compensation terms?
choice_a: Yes -- the statute's compensation-negotiability language expressly contemplates fees being paid by sharing or splitting commissions between brokers
choice_b: No -- commission splitting between brokers is categorically prohibited under Ohio license law
choice_c: No -- only the listing broker may ever receive any portion of the commission proceeds
choice_d: Yes, but only if the county real estate board pre-approves the specific split
explanation: ORC 4735.55's compensation-negotiability disclosure expressly contemplates that fees may be paid by the seller, buyer, landlord, tenant, or a third party, or by sharing or splitting fees and commissions between brokers -- co-brokerage splitting is a disclosed, contemplated option, not a prohibited practice.

question: "Blockbusting," the practice ORC 4735.55 requires every written agency agreement to define and declare illegal, generally refers to what conduct?
choice_a: Inducing property sales by suggesting that a neighborhood's racial, religious, or other protected-class composition is changing in a way that will hurt property values
choice_b: A broker refusing to show properties outside a buyer's pre-approved loan amount
choice_c: Bundling multiple unrelated listings into a single marketing package
choice_d: A zoning-code term describing the consolidation of adjacent parcels
explanation: Blockbusting is the standard real-estate-law term for inducing panic sales by suggesting a neighborhood's protected-class composition is changing to the detriment of property values; ORC 4735.55 requires the written agreement to define this practice and state that it is illegal.
source_note: ORC 4735.55 (disclosure requirement confirmed via direct fetch of codes.ohio.gov; blockbusting's general meaning per standard fair-housing usage)

question: What general purpose do the HUD equal housing opportunity logotype and blockbusting statement required by ORC 4735.55 serve within the written agency agreement?
choice_a: They put clients on direct written notice, at the point they sign a representation agreement, that housing discrimination and blockbusting are illegal, reinforcing fair-housing compliance as part of the disclosure package
choice_b: They establish the broker's personal liability insurance coverage limits
choice_c: They set the geographic boundaries within which the agent may lawfully show property
choice_d: They certify the brokerage's membership in a particular multiple listing service
explanation: By requiring the HUD logotype and blockbusting statement directly inside the signed agreement, ORC 4735.55 ensures every client receives fair-housing notice at the moment they enter into representation, rather than leaving that notice to separate marketing materials.

question: Which of the following is NOT among the disclosure elements ORC 4735.55 requires in a written agency agreement?
choice_a: A statement of the exact dollar amount of commission the broker will earn on the transaction
choice_b: A conspicuous statement that compensation is negotiable and not fixed by law
choice_c: A statement defining blockbusting and declaring it illegal
choice_d: A definite expiration date
explanation: ORC 4735.55 requires disclosure that compensation is negotiable and not fixed by law -- it does not require the agreement to lock in an exact dollar commission figure, since the entire point of the negotiability disclosure is that no fee is preset or mandated.

question: A written listing agreement proposes a flat 6% commission but does not separately state that the figure is negotiable or explain that it is not fixed by law. Does ORC 4735.55 forbid proposing a specific commission percentage in the agreement?
choice_a: No -- ORC 4735.55 does not forbid proposing a specific commission percentage; it requires the agreement to conspicuously disclose that the fee is negotiable and not fixed by law, which can coexist with a proposed starting percentage
choice_b: Yes -- stating any specific numeric commission percentage automatically violates ORC 4735.55
choice_c: Yes -- only a percentage range, never a single flat rate, may lawfully be proposed
choice_d: No, but only because this rule is limited to commercial real estate transactions
explanation: ORC 4735.55 requires that the agreement conspicuously disclose compensation is negotiable and not set by law; it does not bar a broker from proposing a specific starting percentage, so long as the required negotiability disclosure also appears in the agreement.

question: Which Ohio Revised Code section governs written, informed consent to a dual agency relationship, and is therefore NOT the correct citation for the negotiable-compensation, blockbusting, and HUD-logo disclosure requirements?
choice_a: ORC 4735.71, which requires written, informed consent to a dual agency relationship but does not itself contain the negotiable-compensation, blockbusting, or HUD-logo disclosure language
choice_b: ORC 4735.55, which is the correct source for the negotiable-compensation, blockbusting, and HUD-logo disclosure requirements
choice_c: ORC 4735.18(A)(39), which addresses the right-to-list home-sale agreement prohibition
choice_d: ORC 4735.091, which addresses employee/independent-contractor association with a brokerage
explanation: ORC 4735.71 governs dual-agency written consent -- requiring both parties' informed written consent to a dual representation -- and does not itself contain the negotiable-compensation, blockbusting, or HUD-logo disclosure content, which is found in ORC 4735.55.
source_note: ORC 4735.71 (confirmed via direct fetch of codes.ohio.gov; included to clarify what it does NOT cover -- 4735.71 governs dual-agency consent, while the compensation/blockbusting/HUD-logo disclosures are ORC 4735.55)

question: ORC 4735.57's dual-agency disclosure statement requires disclosure of the "source of compensation" to the broker. Does this substitute for ORC 4735.55's negotiable-compensation, blockbusting, and HUD-logo requirements in an ordinary (non-dual-agency) written representation agreement?
choice_a: No -- ORC 4735.57's compensation-source disclosure applies to the dual-agency disclosure statement and does not substitute for the distinct negotiable-compensation, blockbusting, and HUD-logo elements ORC 4735.55 requires in written agency agreements generally
choice_b: Yes -- ORC 4735.57 and ORC 4735.55 are the same statute cited under two different numbers
choice_c: Yes -- once source of compensation is disclosed under 4735.57, no further compensation disclosure is required under any other section
choice_d: No, because ORC 4735.57 has been repealed and its content fully merged into ORC 4735.55
explanation: ORC 4735.57 addresses the separate dual-agency disclosure statement's compensation-source element, which is distinct from -- and does not replace -- ORC 4735.55's independent negotiable-compensation, blockbusting, and HUD-logo requirements for written agency agreements generally.

question: ORC 4735.55's compensation-negotiability disclosure permits fees to be paid by the landlord or the tenant, not only a buyer or seller. In which type of representation agreement does this landlord/tenant language most directly apply?
choice_a: A lease or rental representation agreement, where the compensating party may be the landlord or the tenant rather than a home buyer or seller
choice_b: A purchase agreement only, since landlord/tenant language is surplus with no practical application
choice_c: A property-management trust-account agreement exclusively
choice_d: A right-to-list home-sale agreement exclusively
explanation: ORC 4735.55's disclosure lists the seller, buyer, landlord, tenant, or a third party as possible compensating parties, reflecting that the statute's written-agreement requirements extend to lease and rental representation, not only sale transactions.

question: What must accompany a written agency agreement once it has been fully signed and dated, under ORC 4735.55?
choice_a: A copy of the signed and dated agreement must be provided to the client
choice_b: A copy must be filed with the Ohio Division of Real Estate within 10 days
choice_c: A copy must be recorded with the county recorder of deeds
choice_d: A copy must be forwarded to the administrator of the Ohio Real Estate Recovery Fund
explanation: ORC 4735.55 requires the signed and dated agreement to be provided to the client in copy form -- it does not require filing with the Division of Real Estate, county recording, or transmittal to the Recovery Fund administrator.

question: A brokerage's standard buyer agreement includes the HUD equal housing opportunity logotype and a definite expiration date, but never states whether the buyer's agent's appointment is exclusive or nonexclusive. Is this agreement complete under ORC 4735.55?
choice_a: No -- ORC 4735.55 separately requires the agreement to state that the licensee is appointed as agent and whether that appointment is exclusive or nonexclusive; omitting this element leaves the agreement incomplete even though other required elements are present
choice_b: Yes -- exclusivity language is optional decoration, not a required element under ORC 4735.55
choice_c: Yes -- exclusivity status is implied automatically by the presence of the HUD logotype
choice_d: No, but only because the expiration date is also technically invalid without exclusivity language
explanation: ORC 4735.55 lists the exclusive-or-nonexclusive appointment statement as its own required element, independent of the HUD logotype and expiration-date requirements -- an agreement can satisfy those two elements while still being incomplete for omitting the exclusivity statement.

question: Why does ORC 4735.55 require the blockbusting and HUD equal-housing disclosures to appear directly inside the written agency agreement, rather than leaving fair-housing compliance to be addressed only in separate marketing materials?
choice_a: To ensure every client sees fair-housing and anti-blockbusting notice at the point of signing the document that creates the agency relationship itself, not only if and when marketing materials happen to include such notice
choice_b: Because federal law requires such notices to appear exclusively inside private contracts, never in advertising
choice_c: Because marketing materials are categorically exempt from all Ohio fair-housing law
choice_d: Because the written agency agreement is the only document Ohio law regulates at all
explanation: Embedding the blockbusting and HUD-logo disclosures in the signed agreement itself guarantees the client receives that notice at the moment of engagement, independent of whether or how thoroughly separate marketing materials address fair-housing compliance.

question: A brokerage's independent-contractor salesperson closes a sale, and the broker receives the full commission from escrow. How do ORC 4735.091 and ORC 4735.18(A)(31) apply together to this scenario?
choice_a: ORC 4735.091 permits the independent-contractor structure itself, while ORC 4735.18(A)(31) independently requires the broker, within a reasonable time after receiving the commission, to render an accounting and pay the salesperson's earned share -- regardless of which structure 4735.091 established
choice_b: Only ORC 4735.091 applies; commission payment timing is entirely unregulated for independent contractors
choice_c: Only ORC 4735.18(A)(31) applies; the independent-contractor structure itself is unauthorized without a separate statute
choice_d: The two statutes conflict, and ORC 4735.091 controls, excusing the broker from any accounting duty
explanation: ORC 4735.091 governs the structural classification of the working relationship, while ORC 4735.18(A)(31) imposes a separate, independently enforceable duty to account for and pay earned commissions -- the two statutes operate together, not in conflict, and neither excuses the other.

question: Among ORC 4735.091, ORC 4735.18(A)(31), ORC 4735.18(A)(39), and ORC 4735.55, which one specifically prohibits entering into a named type of listing agreement, as opposed to regulating payment timing, licensee classification, or agreement disclosure content?
choice_a: ORC 4735.18(A)(39), which prohibits entering into a "right-to-list" home sale agreement
choice_b: ORC 4735.091, which prohibits nothing and only authorizes employee/independent-contractor status
choice_c: ORC 4735.18(A)(31), which governs commission accounting and payment timing, not agreement types
choice_d: ORC 4735.55, which governs required disclosure content in written agency agreements, not a prohibited agreement type
explanation: Of the four provisions, only ORC 4735.18(A)(39) prohibits entering into a specifically named type of agreement (the right-to-list home sale agreement); the others authorize a relationship structure, regulate accounting/payment timing, or specify required disclosure content.

question: A written listing agreement (1) has a definite expiration date, discloses commission is negotiable, and includes the HUD logotype and blockbusting statement, but (2) also contains a clause binding the seller to relist with the same broker on the seller's next, unrelated home sale. Which specific provision does clause (2) violate, even though element (1) satisfies ORC 4735.55?
choice_a: ORC 4735.18(A)(39)'s prohibition on entering into a "right-to-list" home sale agreement
choice_b: ORC 4735.091, because the seller was never given an employee/independent-contractor choice
choice_c: ORC 4735.18(A)(31), because no commission had yet been earned on the future sale
choice_d: No provision is violated, since all of ORC 4735.55's disclosure elements were satisfied
explanation: Satisfying ORC 4735.55's disclosure content does not cure a separate, freestanding violation of ORC 4735.18(A)(39) -- binding a seller to relist with the same broker on a future, unrelated sale is exactly the restrictive practice that provision prohibits.

question: A brokerage structures salespersons as independent contractors per ORC 4735.091, uses a fully compliant ORC 4735.55 written agreement with clients, and promptly accounts for and pays commissions per ORC 4735.18(A)(31) -- but every listing agreement includes a right-to-list clause binding sellers to future, unrelated sales. Is this brokerage's practice fully compliant with the four provisions addressed here?
choice_a: No -- despite compliance with ORC 4735.091, ORC 4735.55, and ORC 4735.18(A)(31), the right-to-list clause independently violates ORC 4735.18(A)(39), a separate, freestanding prohibition
choice_b: Yes -- satisfying three of the four provisions is legally sufficient for full compliance
choice_c: Yes -- ORC 4735.18(A)(39) only applies if the broker also violates ORC 4735.18(A)(31) in the same transaction
choice_d: No, but only because independent-contractor status itself is noncompliant with Ohio license law
explanation: Because ORC 4735.18(A)(39) is a standalone, independently enforceable ground, compliance with the other three provisions does not excuse or offset a right-to-list violation -- each provision must be satisfied on its own terms.

question: Of ORC 4735.091, ORC 4735.18(A)(31), ORC 4735.18(A)(39), and ORC 4735.55, which one governs the required content of the written agreement a client signs, rather than the broker-salesperson relationship or a prohibited agreement type?
choice_a: ORC 4735.55, which specifies mandatory disclosure content -- negotiable compensation, blockbusting, HUD logotype, expiration date, exclusivity, fair housing, and signature requirements -- for written agency agreements with clients
choice_b: ORC 4735.091, which governs client-facing disclosure content in written agreements
choice_c: ORC 4735.18(A)(31), which governs client-facing disclosure content in written agreements
choice_d: ORC 4735.18(A)(39), which governs client-facing disclosure content in written agreements
explanation: ORC 4735.55 is the provision that dictates what a written agency agreement with a client must contain; ORC 4735.091 governs the internal broker-licensee relationship structure, ORC 4735.18(A)(31) governs commission accounting/payment between broker and salesperson, and ORC 4735.18(A)(39) prohibits a specific agreement type rather than prescribing disclosure content.

question: ORC 4735.091 and ORC 4735.18(A)(31) both regulate the internal broker-salesperson relationship. Which single provision among the four addressed here instead imposes a client-facing prohibition on a specific type of agreement, rather than governing internal broker-salesperson dealings or written-disclosure content?
choice_a: ORC 4735.18(A)(39), which bars a specific broker-client agreement type -- the "right-to-list" home-sale agreement -- rather than governing internal broker-salesperson relations or disclosure content
choice_b: ORC 4735.091, which bars a specific broker-client agreement type
choice_c: ORC 4735.18(A)(31), which bars a specific broker-client agreement type
choice_d: ORC 4735.55, which bars a specific broker-client agreement type
explanation: Unlike ORC 4735.091 (broker-licensee association structure), ORC 4735.18(A)(31) (broker-salesperson commission accounting/payment), and ORC 4735.55 (required disclosure content), ORC 4735.18(A)(39) stands apart as a direct client-facing prohibition on a specifically named type of agreement.
